How does it work?
Instead of storing your files as bytes, lgit trains a small neural network to memorize them. Each commit is a training run: the network learns to map positional encodings to your data, byte by byte for code or pixel by pixel for images. Checkout is inference: the network reconstructs what it can from its weights
The network uses Fourier positional encoding, ReLU hidden layers, and an Adam optimizer. For text, it outputs a probability distribution over 256 byte values. For images, it predicts RGB values directly. A small network compresses aggressively and hallucinates. A larger one memorizes perfectly but defeats the point
And it all runs in your browser
The fun part is the failures. Run the JS code before and after a commit to see how neural corruption breaks your program in ways that are nothing like traditional file corruption

Are you like me and thought that the Adapter was the Router? Well, no. The adapter is just a WiFi 6E dongle that connects to the headset's own hidden hotspot.
Just here for the tool? Jump to
Want To Try It?
. Here for the story? Keep reading.
Why?
But let's start from the beginning. I wanted to play Half-Life: Alyx on the Frame but forgot the Adapter at someone else's house. I didn't want that to stop me from playing.
The issue is that my home WiFi is just an old GL.iNet travel router which only supports 2.4GHz. With just that it is pretty much impossible to have a good time playing.
The Hotspot Solution
So the first thing I did was to just use the WiFi 6E card on my PC's motherboard. It seemed to work way better but latency spikes still were killing the experience.
The Frame can stream over two WiFi links at the same time (Valve calls this Multilink). As far as I can tell, that's the trick against latency spikes: when one link hiccups, the other one hopefully doesn't hiccup at the exact same moment. With only one link, every single spike ends up right on your face.
So the Frame can do two links, but my PC only has one WiFi card. And I don't own another WiFi 6E card... or so I thought. Turns out laptops have WiFi too. So I grabbed my MacBook and used it as a hotspot while it was connected to my network over Ethernet. In typical Apple fashion this was not as straightforward and very buggy to set up. However once it worked, I had a new AP which I could even move and that was not stuck to an antenna somewhere under my desk.
The "Adapter"
As you might have guessed by now, the MacBook hotspot situation again has only one radio and I had no adapter. So I needed to use the same mechanism as the Adapter to connect my PC's WiFi card to the Frame somehow. At that time I did indeed not know that it is just a hidden hotspot from the Frame side. I searched every settings menu to see if I can change where the second radio connects to, but found nothing.
Luckily the Frame is just Linux. Linux machines normally have terminals. Terminals normally don't hide their secrets. Secrets normally are just a command away.
To make my job even easier, Valve actually gives an option to enable SSH on the Frame.
Once I connected to the Frame via SSH, I found out that
softapmanager
is used and it opened a hidden network called
frame_XXXXXXXX
plus a 32 character password. It uses the separate
wlanap
interface.
On my PC I just connected to that network and it worked... ish?
Multilink Streaming
Streaming via Multilink (so over both radios) worked! But is my motherboard WiFi card now an official Valve adapter? Depends on who you ask.
The Frame has two different places that show the adapter. The first one says Valve's adapter is not connected. Fair enough, it isn't. But once you actually connect and look at the other one, it proudly tells you that you're connected via WiFi and Valve's own adapter!
So the Frame disagrees with itself. And SteamVR? SteamVR said the adapter was connected the whole time. If even the Frame is confused, I don't feel too bad about being confused either.
A Small SteamVR Rant (Feel Free To Skip)
Quick detour before the interesting part. SteamVR on Linux is... an experience.
Connecting, even without my Frankenstein setup, was a pain. Sometimes it took a minute to connect. And every time I pressed the connect button while waiting? Saved up and replayed afterwards. All of them. Great experience!
I've also seen a number of interesting crashes in both SteamVR and Half-Life: Alyx. No idea if that's the Frame or just Linux being Linux. One of them I traced down to a poisoned mutex in Alyx, which then spawned an SDL window, blocking, on the main thread. So the game looked frozen or crashed while it was really just waiting on that window.

So far I knew three things: the Frame has a hidden hotspot, it runs on its own
wlanap
interface, and the Adapter is just a WiFi 6E dongle. What I didn't know: how does Steam know the credentials for that hotspot?
My goal was simple: A tool which connects your PC to the Frame's hidden hotspot, without the Adapter and without SSH. And oh, I am unsure if I would do it again...
Getting the credentials was easy if the Adapter had been connected once, since Steam stores them in a NetworkManager profile. But I wanted them without ever having connected the Adapter.
This is the part where my understanding of how it works changed multiple times!
Down The steamclient.so Rabbit Hole
So I found a really cursed way to get them. The credentials usually get shared via Steam's local Remote Play protocol, and the thing speaking that protocol on your PC is
steamclient.so
. So the plan was: load
steamclient.so
into my own program, connect to the running Steam and just ask it nicely.
Here is how "just ask it nicely" went:
Load
steamclient.so
, call
CreateInterface
, connect to the running Steam over its IPC pipe. So far so good!
Find the methods I need, like
PairViaWifiAP
. They exist! They're just not exported. They live in private C++ interfaces nobody is supposed to touch.
No exports, so I go through the vtable. Object pointer, table of function pointers, pick the right slot, call it and hope.
To find the right functions, read the ELF at runtime and look for the instructions that load the method's name. Then hash every function I call, so I don't accidentally call something else.
Steam updates. 15 of 16 hashes change.
PairViaWifiAP
moves from slot 55 to slot 61.
Add an option to ignore the hashes. Basically a "trust me bro" flag.
Steam beta: "Steam has no
GetRemoteClientCount
". It does! The compiler just loaded the string into
R13
first and then moved it to
RCX
, and my scanner only looked for
RCX
.
Write an actual instruction decoder that follows registers around. In theory it now recognizes every Steam version I could find, going back a year. In theory....
It was a real mess and some of the worst code I have ever written, but it worked. I was able to get the credentials from Steam directly without having the adapter connected!
Works On My Machine
Well, the only problem was that the other machine was also mine.
On my second PC, which never had the Adapter connected, it just didn't work. So I spent a lot of time debugging different
steamclient.so
versions, only to realize that my mental model was fully wrong.

Reality: Steam on my second PC never got the credentials. It never even tried. And my main PC? It just handed me cached credentials from the last time the real Adapter was paired. So my "it works!" was actually "it remembers!".

Looking back, two error messages should have tipped me off way earlier.
The first time I talked the Remote Play protocol myself, I got: "unauthorized". Fair. Just being on the same LAN doesn't mean you get to mess with someone's hotspot. You need to be paired.

Turns out that neither the Frame nor the adapter is responsible for setting up the credentials. It is Steam itself. Wait for the Frame to confirm it actually took them.

Your PC already paired with the Frame in Steam
The Frame awake and on the same LAN as your PC
Rust, OpenSSL 3 development libraries and
pkg-config
to build it (or just download it from actions)

./target/release/steamframe-link set-creds

Heads up:

changes the Frame's hotspot and can interrupt its current wireless connection.
The profile on your PC doesn't become your default route, so your normal internet keeps working while you're connected to the Frame.
All the other options
Passwords

Saved credentials
live in

(default

). They're saved
before

.

the tool only treats credentials as set when the Frame answers with success or reports the matching network hash. A disconnect or timeout is never success, and

Several Frames:

Discovery blocked?

--no-autoconnect

--wpa2

A live map you can rewind, that tells you where every contact came from.
There is no shortage of dashboards that draw aircraft and ships on a globe.
Nearly all of them are stateless viewers of somebody else's API: they show you
this instant, they cannot show you last Tuesday, and they render whatever the
upstream asserts without saying who saw it or how long ago. Velocity is
self-hosted and keyless like those, and then does the two things they don't.
It keeps history you own.
Flightradar24 gates replay at 7 days free,
MarineTraffic cut its free window to 24 hours, ADS-B Exchange killed its free

archive is a Postgres + TimescaleDB hypertable (

long as you give it room, with a scrubber to rewind to any past moment, and
SQLite remains the keyless fallback when no
HISTORY_PG_DSN
is set. No
account, no API key, nobody who can paywall, filter or cut off your archive.

was ever broadcast. So every contact carries which independent sources reported
it, how many agreed, and how old the fix actually is — with the confidence rule
written out rather than implied. Cached sources report the age of the
data
,

Take the tour
1. The whole planet, live.
Thousands of aircraft plus vessels, satellites,
quakes and more on one Cesium globe. Every aircraft and ship renders as its
category icon, coloured and rotated to its heading; dense areas cluster into
count badges you can drill into.
2. Zoom anywhere, toggle everything.
Drag into a region and traffic, labels
and coastlines fill in. The left rail is the whole intel stack in one tree — air,
maritime, space, ground hazards, signals and 18 infrastructure layers — each
with its live count. A right-side map toolbar adds the analyst verbs on top of
the globe:
measure
a running great-circle distance,
area-select
a box
and search every object inside it,
annotate
with dropped markers, or
move
a marker — plus one-click camera reset and zoom.
3. Click anything.
Select an aircraft or vessel and the right panel fills
with its dossier: identity, kinematics, the flight/route, ACARS, a
pattern-of-life baseline, GPS integrity and the raw fields — while a magenta
line traces its recent track on the globe. An
AI assessment
block (labelled,
and grounded in the observed track) summarises what the dossier fields imply.
Click empty space and it all clears.
4. Or query the whole store at once.
The Explorer app is every live object
in one filterable, sortable table — tens of thousands of tracks across vessels,
aircraft and quakes, each tagged with the feed it came from and how long ago it
was seen. Facet it, save the search, export the result to CSV.
5. Chokepoints and AOIs, watched continuously.
A curated library of the
world's maritime chokepoints — Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb, Malacca, the Taiwan
Strait, the English Channel, undersea-cable corridors — each with live transit
counts and the daily oil-flow figures that make it matter. Standing detections
fire against them in the background.
6. Airspace, bases, ports and airports — operational context, still keyless.
Toggle the TFR/Airspace layer and live FAA temporary flight restrictions draw as
real polygons, coloured by reason with their altitude bands. Alongside them:
7,183 military bases (air, naval and army, from Wikidata), NGA NAVAREA broadcast
warnings with mine areas flagged, 3,804 ports from the NGA World Port Index
(harbour size and type, shelter, repairs, dry dock, pier and channel depths),
and airports enriched with runways (length, surface, lighting, per-end ILS
category from FAA NASR), tower/ground/ATIS frequencies, live METAR with flight
category, and a LiveATC linkout. A basemap picker swaps between nine keyless
map styles (Carto dark, 3D satellite + terrain, Apple satellite, Esri
imagery/topo/dark, OpenTopoMap, USGS, Sentinel-2 cloudless), each probed live
before it's offered and each carrying its required attribution.
7. Space, with real physics.
~16k satellites from CelesTrak, propagated
in-browser with actual SGP4 orbital mechanics and enriched from SATCAT with
owner, launch date, radar cross-section and orbit class.
8. The watch officer works the inbox.
An autonomous watch officer fuses
jamming, dark vessels, military air activity and conflict events into ranked,
cited alerts — GPS spoofing, jamming cells, dark-vessel candidates — each with an
[inferred]
reasoning line and a one-click
slew to
. It runs
detect_deception
and
deep_analyze
against the live picture, so the inbox fills itself on a fresh
keyless boot with no operator setup.
9. …and writes the brief.
Every couple of minutes it promotes the
convergences — "vessels went dark near reported activity", "spoofed tracks
co-located with an AIS gap" — into ranked incident cards with a written, cited
summary and a
slew to
button. Actionable incidents are auto-promoted into the
investigation graph, so the ontology grows itself.
10. Keep it as evidence.
Anything worth keeping goes into the
chain-of-custody
evidence locker
: capture a URL snapshot, upload a file, grab
a screenshot, or freeze the current feed state, and each artifact is hashed with
SHA-256, written to
./data/evidence
, and logged to an append-only custody
chain in the local ontology store. Attach it to a situation, re-verify the hash
any time, or roll a whole case into a signed hash-of-hashes manifest. Fully
keyless. From there,
Reports
exports the case (see
Export
) as a
JSON bundle, a self-contained HTML report with per-claim provenance footnotes,
or a PPTX brief — with any AI narrative confined to a clearly labelled block.
11. A tool that draws on the map gets its own window.
The annotation
editor, the watchbox rules and the field kit open as free-floating, draggable,
resizable windows over the globe rather than stealing the rail from the layer
tree — arm a tool from the map toolbar, set up what it draws beside the thing
you are drawing on, and
Window → Re-dock every floating panel
clears them all.
Positions persist for the session.
12. Bring your own data — the Foundry tab.
Upload a CSV/JSON/NDJSON, shape it
through a governed pipeline (13 transform steps: filter, derive, join, aggregate,
union, window, pivot, dedup, cast, sort…), gate every version with data-health
checks (freshness SLAs, schema-drift, uniqueness…), and bind it into the same
ontology graph as the live feeds. Lineage, immutable versions with rollback, and
a dead-letter for rows that fail a transform all come along; the pipeline graph
flags exactly which outputs went stale.
13. Automate it — the Workflows tab.
A node-graph editor over the same live
feeds and ontology: wire sources (aircraft, vessels, quakes, alerts, datasets,
ontology, countries) through sandboxed Python/SQL/LLM transform blocks into sinks
(alerts, ontology objects, datasets, persistent memory), then run it on a
schedule. Control blocks can reach outward too — webhooks to your own server, or
a MAVLink bridge for drone tasking that rehearses log-only without a vehicle.
Scope and limits
The point is fusion. Plenty of sites already do one feed well: Flightradar24 for
planes, MarineTraffic for ships,
GPSJam
for jamming.
Velocity goes after the seam between them: AIS plus radar imagery flags a ship
that's switched its transponder off; a cluster of aircraft reporting bad GPS
integrity becomes a jamming hotspot; when two or more of those line up in the
same place and time, they get promoted to a single incident with a written,
cited summary.
A few things worth knowing up front, because I'd rather you read them here than
be annoyed later:
It's built for one analyst. One optional API key, no accounts or roles.

— only materializes when no

Volatile, and cleared on backend restart: the live incident list, transient
AOI selections, and generated watch-officer briefs. The Docker Compose
volumes mean the durable stores survive
docker compose down
, not just a
process restart.
Retention, honestly.
The dev compose sets
HISTORY_RETENTION_HOURS=48
(2 days), but that's a ceiling, not a promise:
HISTORY_MAX_BYTES
(2 GB by
default) binds first, and at measured global ADS-B+AIS ingest (~3 GB/h on a
keyless box pulling full-breadth feeds) the byte cap fills well before the
hour window matters, leaving well under 2 hours of effective depth out of
the box — not 48. The hour window only becomes the binding limit once disk
is large enough for it to be the tighter cap; a genuine 48h global archive
needs on the order of 150 GB (
~3 GB/h * 48h
). Raise
HISTORY_MAX_BYTES
,
or set
ARCHIVE_MODE=1
with
HISTORY_DISK_BUDGET_GB
sized to what you're
willing to spend on disk (the production compose profile does this, 5 GB to
start).
/api/history/coverage
reports the ACTUAL current depth
(
oldest_ts
), not the configured ceiling, and the 2D console's day-picker
and ownership chip render it, so you can see what you're really getting.
Depth answers now come from the hourly
positions_hourly
aggregate; the old
SQLite coverage scan took 73 s over 78M fixes, which is why the rollup
exists.
AIS runs keyless and global (~50k vessels tracked, MMSI-deduped across
ShipXplorer, MyShipTracking, Digitraffic and Kystverket), but coverage is densest over
Northern Europe and the Baltic and thins out elsewhere; an AISStream key fills
in the gaps. Sparse regions still lean on the radar (SAR) layer.
The two headless-Chrome sidecars are degraded under Docker, not crashed.
ADS-B (OpenSky + the httpx tar1090 mirrors + ShipXplorer AIS) and the
regional Kystverket/Digitraffic AIS feeds are direct HTTP calls and run at
full strength in the container. But the tar1090 ADS-B sidecar and
MyShipTracking (the enabled primary keyless
wide-area
AIS source) drive a
real Chromium via Node, which the slim API image doesn't ship — they log a
warning and sit idle rather than crash the backend, so you lose their extra
coverage, not the app. Run bare-metal (
bash scripts/run-api.sh
) for full
sidecar coverage.

What is enforced
Not promises, checks in the tree. Each line names the route or test that holds
it:
Clearance on reads and writes.
One predicate,
intel/ontology.visible_to
, filters local reads (
get
,
list_by_kind
,
search
, links, assertions) and the situations, maps and evidence routes by
the caller's level and compartments; keyless callers are clearance 0, and a
write above clearance or onto a hidden row answers 403.
→
apps/api/tests/test_clearance_local_reads.py
Custody-chained evidence.
Every capture is hashed with SHA-256 and
appended to an immutable custody log;
GET /api/evidence/{sha}/verify
re-checks the bytes. →
apps/api/tests/test_evidence.py
Hash-chained audit.
Mutations append to
action_log.db
;
GET /api/audit/verify
walks the chain. →
apps/api/tests/test_asvs_fix_a_logging.py
Citations withheld when ungrounded.
LLM_REQUIRE_CITATIONS=1
(default)
withholds a selection or country brief that cites none of its own ids;
GET /api/ai/guardrails
reports the posture. →
apps/api/tests/test_citations_hard.py
Human-in-the-loop write-back.
A write-back action is operator-only and
runs only from a proposal the operator approves; the audit row carries the
payload's SHA-256, never the payload. →
apps/api/tests/test_writeback_action.py

If you run an ADS-B receiver (readsb, ultrafeeder, tar1090), Velocity folds its

in
.env
at your
tar1090's
aircraft.json
. The variable replaces the default list, so keep the

MCP server: query the live console from an AI agent
The part I think is genuinely new: the backend doubles as a
Model Context
Protocol
server, so an AI agent can interrogate the same warm feeds the globe
renders without scraping a dozen sites or flooding its own context. Ask "where
is GPS being jammed right now?" and it answers from the live feed. Full
architecture +
/api/intel/*
HTTP reference:
docs/mcp-server.md
.
It exposes 94 tools over
app.mcp_server
(a representative slice below; run
--list-tools
for the full set):
Tool
What it returns
get_situation
Global summary: aircraft by category, GNSS-degraded count, emergencies, worst jamming cells, vessel/alert counts. The cheap first call.
focus_area(lat,lon,radius_nm)
Loads a region PRIMARY
(dedicated fresh
/v2/point
fetch + ongoing priority refresh, independent of global rate limits) and returns a full bundle: aircraft + density + GPS jamming + vessels + fused anomalies.
aircraft_density
Grid of cells (count, by category, GNSS-degraded) for an area.
gps_jamming
GPSJam-method assessment (ADS-B NACp<8 / NIC<7, 1° bins): flagged cells, severity, affected aircraft. Global or scoped.
query_aircraft
Filtered query (bbox/centre, category, squawk, callsign, altitude band, emergency / gnss_degraded / on_ground).
lookup_aircraft(ident)
One aircraft by ICAO24 or callsign + integrity/threat assessment.
query_vessels
AIS vessels in an area, classified;
dark_only
for dark-vessel candidates.
anomalies
Fused report: emergencies, jamming hotspots, dark vessels, alerts + a triage threat level.
detect_deception
/
locate_emitter
Flag spoofed/co-located tracks; triangulate a jamming source from degraded-integrity aircraft.
whats_changed
/
incident_history
Delta since a timestamp; the incident timeline for an area.
deep_analyze(question, lat?, lon?)
Gathers the relevant intel JSON and has a
reasoning model
reason over it (DeepSeek when configured, else a local Ollama model), so heavy analysis stays off the agent's context and only the conclusion returns.
Every tool returns compact, bounded JSON (counts, grids, ≤50-item samples), so
an agent can sweep the planet for a few hundred tokens instead of pulling 15k
features. Heavy tools also take
detail='short'
(the default digest — top-N
of each list plus a
<field>_total
) or
detail='long'
(the full bundle), so
an agent sweeps in
short
and drills in
long
. Area-primary loading means the
agent's region of interest stays fresh and dense even while the global firehose is
being rate-limited; the rest of the world keeps streaming from the sticky snapshot.

System requirements
The heavy component is the
client
, a CesiumJS WebGL2 globe. It is GPU- and
browser-main-thread-bound, and the backend is light. WebGL2 is required
(Chrome/Edge 110+, Firefox 110+). On hybrid-graphics laptops, force the discrete
GPU (
chrome://gpu
, look for adapter "ACTIVE").
VRAM depends heavily on which mode you run:
2D-dark (default basemap):
light. The globe is a proxied 2D raster basemap
plus the entity layers (aircraft/vessels). Runs on integrated graphics / ~2–4 GB
VRAM, which is the right mode for modest hardware.
3D-sat (satellite imagery + world terrain + OSM 3D buildings, optional Google
Photorealistic 3D):
VRAM-heavy.
CesiumJS streams terrain meshes, high-res
imagery, and 3D-tile building/photogrammetry sets, and it caches into whatever
VRAM is available, measured at
20+ GB on a 32 GB card
. Tilesets are now
individually cache-capped (Google 3D ~1.5 GB, OSM buildings ~0.5 GB) and MSAA is
off (FXAA instead), but with terrain + global imagery + a high-DPI/4K canvas the
resident set is still large. On a card with less VRAM, Cesium evicts and
re-fetches more aggressively (lower fps, more pop-in) and still runs.

All feeds + browser sidecars + 3D-sat terrain + buildings; best frame rate.
These tiers come from a cgroup-isolated benchmark (
tools/perf/bench_ram.sh
)
that constrains backend + Vite + Chrome inside a single MemoryMax and measures
real fps, renderMs, entity counts, and OOM kills at each RAM level. 3D-sat
genuinely wants a lot of VRAM, and the low-VRAM minimum only holds for the
2D-dark map; switch on 3D-sat and you'll want a discrete card with headroom.
Backend (server):
Python 3.12, outbound HTTPS. The
lite
profile
(default) disables browser sidecars, history, and the FR24/OpenSky-gaps tiers,
measuring ~530 MB steady-state RSS — comfortably fits an 8 GB box alongside
the browser. The
full
profile with all direct feeds warm measures ~3.2 GB.
The optional headless-Chrome coverage sidecars are the real memory line item:
the ADS-B scraping tier measured ~11 GB RSS across its ~50-process Chrome tree
and the AIS tier ~3-6 GB across its ~20-36 (both measured 2026-07-24 at full
coverage), so budget roughly 15 GB on top of the backend when both are
enabled — or keep
lite
and use the direct feeds.

Frontend
: Vite + React 18 + TypeScript + CesiumJS + MapLibre GL JS v5.24 + Tailwind + Zustand
Backend
: FastAPI (Python 3.12) + httpx + websockets. Live
derived
state
is in-process (bounded observation store + disk tile cache); durable state
(the position-track replay archive, the ontology store: objects / case files /
situations, and the evidence locker's custody chain) persists to
Postgres + TimescaleDB or SQLite, on Docker volumes in Compose, with a
rolling window by default or an open-ended disk-budgeted archive via
ARCHIVE_MODE
Agent access
: Model Context Protocol server (
app.mcp_server
, MCP SDK) + optional local Ollama analysis
Data
: PostgreSQL 16 + TimescaleDB backs the position archive today (6 hour
chunks, columnar compression, hourly
positions_hourly
rollup, SQLite as the
keyless fallback). PostGIS + Redis remain planned.
Infra
: Docker Compose, nginx reverse proxy

Table of Contents
Table of Contents
A devbox task or app that asks for `gpu="AppleSilicon"` now runs natively on your Mac, so `torch.device("mps")` and MLX work the way `"cuda"` does on a cluster.
The Flyte devbox is where I iterate on ML code before it goes anywhere near a cluster: `flyte start devbox`, write a task, run it, look at it in the console. On an Apple Silicon Mac there's been one glaring gap. The devbox runs every task and app in a container, and on a Mac that container is a Linux VM. Linux has no Metal, so `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` is `False` in there, MLX doesn't run at all, and the 40-core GPU on my laptop sits idle while my training loop crawls along on the CPU.
So we added an Apple Silicon accelerator to the devbox. You ask for it the way you'd ask for an A100:
Copied to clipboard!
env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
name="apple-silicon-train",
image=flyte.Image.from_debian_base().with_pip_packages("torch", "torchvision"),
resources=flyte.Resources(cpu=2, memory="4Gi", gpu="AppleSilicon"),
)
and start the devbox with one flag:
Copied to clipboard!
flyte start devbox --apple-silicon
That's the whole API. `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()` is the same request if you prefer the device helpers (`flyte.GPU`, `flyte.TPU`, `flyte.AMD_GPU`).
What actually runs where
The obvious design is to pass the GPU through to the container. That isn't possible: there's no Metal inside a Linux VM to pass anything to. An earlier version of this work kept the task in its container and gave it a host-side MLX model server to call over HTTP. That's useful if all you want is completions, but it means your code can't touch the GPU itself. You can't move a PyTorch model to `mps`, you can't train, and you can't load an arbitrary Hugging Face model.
So the default is the other way around.
The workload's code runs natively on the Mac
, and the container becomes its proxy:
The container starts as usual. Its Flyte entrypoint (`a0` for tasks, `fserve` for apps) sees that the backend scheduled it as an Apple Silicon workload and hands its own invocation to a bridge that `flyte start devbox --apple-silicon` runs on the host.
The bridge builds a cached `uv` environment for macOS from the image's pip packages, rewrites the in-cluster endpoints to the devbox ports the Mac can reach, and runs the same entrypoint there.
The container streams the host process's log, mirrors its exit code, forwards aborts, and for apps forwards its port, so the console, the run's logs and the app URL behave as they would for any other workload.
From the console's perspective, a task ran in a pod and produced outputs. From the Mac's perspective, a Python process ran in `~/.flyte/apple-silicon/envs/...` with the GPU right there.
On the backend side, a pod that requests the `APPLE_SILICON` device class gets no GPU resource request (no device plugin could satisfy it, so it would sit `Pending` forever) and no GPU node affinity. Instead it gets the bridge's endpoint and a per-workload HMAC token, so one workload can't talk to another's process.
Training on mps from a task
Once the code is on the Mac, the training loop is ordinary PyTorch. The only Apple-specific line is the device:
Copied to clipboard!
@env.task
async def train(epochs: int = 3, batch_size: int = 256, lr: float = 1e-3) -> tuple[dict, flyte.io.File]:
import torch
...
# On a cluster this would be "cuda"; on the Mac's GPU it is "mps". Fail rather than train on the CPU.

Proving it's the GPU
"It feels faster" isn't evidence, so the SDK ships a proof task (`examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_proof/`) that fails unless five checks pass. Because the code runs on the Mac, it can gather the evidence itself:
Where it ran:
`platform` reports `Darwin arm64`, not the container's Linux.
What GPU:

The tradeoffs
Running workload code natively on your Mac means running it
outside any sandbox
. That's the price of real GPU access, and it's why `--apple-silicon` is opt-in. When you pass it, the devbox publishes every port on `127.0.0.1` only, so nothing else on your network can submit a workload that ends up running on your laptop. If you resume a paused Apple Silicon devbox, its bridge comes back without the flag; if the existing devbox was published on every interface, it refuses and tells you to recreate it. The rest of the sharp edges:
No silent CPU fallback.

Only pip packages carry over.
The Mac's environment is built from the image's pip packages, not the image itself, so apt packages and anything else baked into the image aren't there, and neither are k8s-mounted secrets.
It's the devbox, not a cluster.
The accelerator is never cluster-schedulable, and a single workload can't claim more than the Mac's one GPU (`AppleSilicon:2` is rejected).
Several at once share one GPU.
Each Apple Silicon workload is its own process on the Mac, so a fan-out works: `examples/accelerators/apple_silicon_fanout.py` ran eight training shards concurrently. They time-share the GPU, though. Memory is the real ceiling: every process loads its own torch, Metal context and model.
"mps" on the devbox, "cuda" on a cluster.
The program doesn't move between them unchanged: you change the resource request and the device string. Everything around them stays the same: inputs, outputs, caching, logs and app URLs all go through the devbox exactly as they do on a cluster.

The local tier of the "same program, laptop to cluster" loop finally includes the GPU most of us are actually carrying around. To recap:

`flyte.Resources(gpu="AppleSilicon")` or `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()`.

Use it:

Trust it:
a named error instead of a CPU fallback, and a proof task that checks the GPU did the work.

Instead of storing your files as bytes, lgit trains a small neural network to memorize them. Instead of storing your files as bytes, lgit trains a small neural network to memorize them. each layer. If the ANE was requested but cannot be set up, startup fails
rather than quietly falling back to the GPU.
If an ANE call fails during a request, the supervisor records the failure.

Objective-C wrapper over Apple's private ANE runtime. It compiles one ANE

block of up to 16 next tokens. The main model then

experts per layer instead of 8. The scheduler (

decoding would be faster.

that wasn't guessed or whose expert is still on disk. It plans the same
routes as the CPU would; the tests check this end to end, by comparing
speculative output with plain decoding.
The drafter's inputs never pass through the CPU.
The main model copies
the six hidden-state layers the drafter reads into a ring buffer on the GPU,
as part of each layer's work.
One wait per step.
Behind each verify, on the GPU, the drafter adds the
verified tokens to its context, compares its drafts with the main model's
choices, moves to the main model's next token and drafts the next block. The
next verify reads that block straight from the drafter's buffer.

The drafter's 4-bit weights are installed
once into a file and read in place, like the experts.

token's position and the token (the Gumbel-max trick, an exact sample from

noise, so a draft is kept exactly when it equals the main model's own draw.

A TUI and a CLI that help you configure your server to stop bad bots without hiding behind a

Preventative - It downloads known bot lists and IP ranges and blocks them. I particularly
recommend using Geo-blocking. For private servers, you can use an allowlist and block more than
90% of all attacks.

means a few packets will reach your server before they are detected, but at least it will stop
them from escalating.

are always tested before application and it tries to recognize apps running behind HTTP proxies and
adapts the dynamic detection rules to the apps.

A TUI and a CLI that help you configure your server to stop bad bots without hiding behind a
CDN. It is a fancy UI for your existing web server (nginx, Apache or Traefik) and your

one company the keys to all kingdoms.

Preventative - It downloads known bot lists and IP ranges and blocks them. I particularly
recommend using Geo-blocking. For private servers, you can use an allowlist and block more than
90% of all attacks.

means a few packets will reach your server before they are detected, but at least it will stop
them from escalating.

tries
to keep you from doing something self-destructive. You will always see what changes
first before you apply it, and you can use the

are always tested before application and it tries to recognize apps running behind HTTP proxies and

This tool edits your web server config and your firewall, and you use it at your own risk.

How it compares
Stop Bots covers ground that usually takes two or three tools: blocking at the HTTP layer in
the web server, at the IP layer in the firewall, and detection from your logs. It does this in
one local binary, with a screen to review and undo every block. It doesn't need an account or a
cloud service, and it doesn't send anything about your traffic anywhere.
fail2ban

Are you like me and thought that the Adapter was the Router? Well, no. The adapter is just a WiFi 6E dongle that connects to the headset's own hidden hotspot.

The Hotspot Solution
So the first thing I did was to just use the WiFi 6E card on my PC's motherboard. It seemed to work way better but latency spikes still were killing the experience.
The Frame can stream over two WiFi links at the same time (Valve calls this Multilink). As far as I can tell, that's the trick against latency spikes: when one link hiccups, the other one hopefully doesn't hiccup at the exact same moment. With only one link, every single spike ends up right on your face.
So the Frame can do two links, but my PC only has one WiFi card. And I don't own another WiFi 6E card... or so I thought. Turns out laptops have WiFi too. So I grabbed my MacBook and used it as a hotspot while it was connected to my network over Ethernet. In typical Apple fashion this was not as straightforward and very buggy to set up. However once it worked, I had a new AP which I could even move and that was not stuck to an antenna somewhere under my desk.
The "Adapter"
As you might have guessed by now, the MacBook hotspot situation again has only one radio and I had no adapter. So I needed to use the same mechanism as the Adapter to connect my PC's WiFi card to the Frame somehow. At that time I did indeed not know that it is just a hidden hotspot from the Frame side. I searched every settings menu to see if I can change where the second radio connects to, but found nothing.
Luckily the Frame is just Linux. Linux machines normally have terminals. Terminals normally don't hide their secrets. Secrets normally are just a command away.
To make my job even easier, Valve actually gives an option to enable SSH on the Frame.
Once I connected to the Frame via SSH, I found out that
softapmanager

frame_XXXXXXXX

wlanap
interface.

Multilink Streaming
Streaming via Multilink (so over both radios) worked! But is my motherboard WiFi card now an official Valve adapter? Depends on who you ask.
The Frame has two different places that show the adapter. The first one says Valve's adapter is not connected. Fair enough, it isn't. But once you actually connect and look at the other one, it proudly tells you that you're connected via WiFi and Valve's own adapter!
So the Frame disagrees with itself. And SteamVR? SteamVR said the adapter was connected the whole time. If even the Frame is confused, I don't feel too bad about being confused either.

Connecting, even without my Frankenstein setup, was a pain. Sometimes it took a minute to connect. And every time I pressed the connect button while waiting? Saved up and replayed afterwards. All of them. Great experience!

So the game looked frozen or crashed while it was really just waiting on that window.

wlanap

steamclient.so

Load
steamclient.so

CreateInterface

Find the methods I need, like

No exports, so I go through the vtable. Object pointer, table of function pointers, pick the right slot, call it and hope.
To find the right functions, read the ELF at runtime and look for the instructions that load the method's name. Then hash every function I call, so I don't accidentally call something else.
Steam updates. 15 of 16 hashes change.
PairViaWifiAP
moves from slot 55 to slot 61.
Add an option to ignore the hashes. Basically a "trust me bro" flag.

GetRemoteClientCount

R13
first and then moved it to
RCX

RCX
.

steamclient.so

The first time I talked the Remote Play protocol myself, I got: "unauthorized". Fair. Just being on the same LAN doesn't mean you get to mess with someone's hotspot. You need to be paired.

steamclient.so
code? Gone. Deleted. Never to be seen again, I hated it anyways.

Find the Frame on your normal LAN, the same way Steam does.

Wait for the Frame to confirm it actually took them.

The profile on your PC doesn't become your default route, so your normal internet keeps working while you're connected to the Frame.

live in

Several Frames:

Was it faster than just picking up the Adapter from where I left it? No. Not even close.

But let's start from the beginning. I wanted to play Half-Life: Alyx on the Frame but forgot the Adapter at someone else's house. I didn't want that to stop me from playing.
The issue is that my home WiFi is just an old GL.iNet travel router which only supports 2.4GHz. With just that it is pretty much impossible to have a good time playing.
The Hotspot Solution
So the first thing I did was to just use the WiFi 6E card on my PC's motherboard. It seemed to work way better but latency spikes still were killing the experience.
The Frame can stream over two WiFi links at the same time (Valve calls this Multilink). As far as I can tell, that's the trick against latency spikes: when one link hiccups, the other one hopefully doesn't hiccup at the exact same moment. With only one link, every single spike ends up right on your face.
So the Frame can do two links, but my PC only has one WiFi card. And I don't own another WiFi 6E card... or so I thought. Turns out laptops have WiFi too. So I grabbed my MacBook and used it as a hotspot while it was connected to my network over Ethernet. In typical Apple fashion this was not as straightforward and very buggy to set up. However once it worked, I had a new AP which I could even move and that was not stuck to an antenna somewhere under my desk.
The "Adapter"
As you might have guessed by now, the MacBook hotspot situation again has only one radio and I had no adapter. So I needed to use the same mechanism as the Adapter to connect my PC's WiFi card to the Frame somehow. At that time I did indeed not know that it is just a hidden hotspot from the Frame side. I searched every settings menu to see if I can change where the second radio connects to, but found nothing.
Luckily the Frame is just Linux. Linux machines normally have terminals. Terminals normally don't hide their secrets. Secrets normally are just a command away.
To make my job even easier, Valve actually gives an option to enable SSH on the Frame.
Once I connected to the Frame via SSH, I found out that
softapmanager
is used and it opened a hidden network called
frame_XXXXXXXX
plus a 32 character password. It uses the separate
wlanap
interface.
On my PC I just connected to that network and it worked... ish?
Multilink Streaming
Streaming via Multilink (so over both radios) worked! But is my motherboard WiFi card now an official Valve adapter? Depends on who you ask.
The Frame has two different places that show the adapter. The first one says Valve's adapter is not connected. Fair enough, it isn't. But once you actually connect and look at the other one, it proudly tells you that you're connected via WiFi and Valve's own adapter!
So the Frame disagrees with itself. And SteamVR? SteamVR said the adapter was connected the whole time. If even the Frame is confused, I don't feel too bad about being confused either.
A Small SteamVR Rant (Feel Free To Skip)
Quick detour before the interesting part. SteamVR on Linux is... an experience.
Connecting, even without my Frankenstein setup, was a pain. Sometimes it took a minute to connect. And every time I pressed the connect button while waiting? Saved up and replayed afterwards. All of them. Great experience!
I've also seen a number of interesting crashes in both SteamVR and Half-Life: Alyx. No idea if that's the Frame or just Linux being Linux. One of them I traced down to a poisoned mutex in Alyx, which then spawned an SDL window, blocking, on the main thread. So the game looked frozen or crashed while it was really just waiting on that window.
Okay, rant over. Back to the WiFi.
Okay, this is nice, but how does it work?
So far I knew three things: the Frame has a hidden hotspot, it runs on its own
wlanap
interface, and the Adapter is just a WiFi 6E dongle. What I didn't know: how does Steam know the credentials for that hotspot?
My goal was simple: A tool which connects your PC to the Frame's hidden hotspot, without the Adapter and without SSH. And oh, I am unsure if I would do it again...
Getting the credentials was easy if the Adapter had been connected once, since Steam stores them in a NetworkManager profile. But I wanted them without ever having connected the Adapter.
This is the part where my understanding of how it works changed multiple times!
Down The steamclient.so Rabbit Hole
So I found a really cursed way to get them. The credentials usually get shared via Steam's local Remote Play protocol, and the thing speaking that protocol on your PC is
steamclient.so
. So the plan was: load
steamclient.so
into my own program, connect to the running Steam and just ask it nicely.
Here is how "just ask it nicely" went:
Load
steamclient.so
, call
CreateInterface
, connect to the running Steam over its IPC pipe. So far so good!
Find the methods I need, like
PairViaWifiAP
. They exist! They're just not exported. They live in private C++ interfaces nobody is supposed to touch.
No exports, so I go through the vtable. Object pointer, table of function pointers, pick the right slot, call it and hope.
To find the right functions, read the ELF at runtime and look for the instructions that load the method's name. Then hash every function I call, so I don't accidentally call something else.
Steam updates. 15 of 16 hashes change.
PairViaWifiAP
moves from slot 55 to slot 61.
Add an option to ignore the hashes. Basically a "trust me bro" flag.
Steam beta: "Steam has no
GetRemoteClientCount
". It does! The compiler just loaded the string into
R13
first and then moved it to
RCX
, and my scanner only looked for
RCX
.
Write an actual instruction decoder that follows registers around. In theory it now recognizes every Steam version I could find, going back a year. In theory....
It was a real mess and some of the worst code I have ever written, but it worked. I was able to get the credentials from Steam directly without having the adapter connected!
Works On My Machine
Well, the only problem was that the other machine was also mine.
On my second PC, which never had the Adapter connected, it just didn't work. So I spent a lot of time debugging different
steamclient.so
versions, only to realize that my mental model was fully wrong.
My mental model: the Frame owns the password, and Steam asks for it. So I just had to find the asking part.
Reality: Steam on my second PC never got the credentials. It never even tried. And my main PC? It just handed me cached credentials from the last time the real Adapter was paired. So my "it works!" was actually "it remembers!".
The Clue
Looking back, two error messages should have tipped me off way earlier.
The first time I talked the Remote Play protocol myself, I got: "unauthorized". Fair. Just being on the same LAN doesn't mean you get to mess with someone's hotspot. You need to be paired.
Much later I came back with proper authentication and asked again. This time it didn't say "unauthorized". It said: "No dongle present."
Not "here is your password". Not "go away". "No dongle present." As if the dongle had to bring something to the table... Oh fuck wait!?
Reverse Flow For Credentials
Turns out that neither the Frame nor the adapter is responsible for setting up the credentials. It is Steam itself. Steam derives an SSID and password using information from the adapter and sends them to the Frame via the Remote Play protocol. The Frame then sets up its hotspot with those credentials.
So all I had to do was the same thing Steam does, just without the adapter. By default the tool generates a random SSID and password, but you can also pick your own and use your creativity!
Interestingly enough, this works the exact opposite way of how the Frame WiFi works itself. The Frame opens the AP and the adapter connects to it. Normally the access point picks the credentials and the clients join. Here, the PC decides, and the Frame, the actual AP, just hosts whatever it's told.
How It Works Now
All that cursed
steamclient.so
code? Gone. Deleted. Never to be seen again, I hated it anyways.
Instead, it just speaks the Remote Play LAN protocol itself:
Find the Frame on your normal LAN, the same way Steam does.
Connect using the keys Steam already saved when you paired your PC with the Frame. So yes, you still need to pair them in Steam once.
Tell the Frame "yes, I totally have a dongle". There is literally a
wifi_dongle_present
flag for that.
Hand it an SSID and password.
Wait for the Frame to confirm it actually took them.
After that, NetworkManager connects your WiFi card to the Frame's new hotspot. No dongle, no SSH, no reading assembly at runtime.
Want To Try It?
You need:
Linux with NetworkManager
A WiFi card that can do 6GHz and WPA3, and a regulatory domain that allows it. The Frame's hotspot used 6GHz, 160MHz and WPA3-SAE in my setup, so an old 2.4GHz card won't cut it.
Steam running with Remote Play enabled, as the same user that runs the tool
Your PC already paired with the Frame in Steam
The Frame awake and on the same LAN as your PC
Rust, OpenSSL 3 development libraries and

Heads up:

The profile on your PC doesn't become your default route, so your normal internet keeps working while you're connected to the Frame.
All the other options

live in

(default
~/.local/state/steamframe-link/

before
sending, so a dropped connection can't lose a generated password. Retry them with

.
Confirmation:
the tool only treats credentials as set when the Frame answers with success or reports the matching network hash. A disconnect or timeout is never success, and
setup
refuses unconfirmed credentials.
Several Frames:
use the ID from

with
--client ID
. (If you really have multiply, why not send one to me? 🫣)
Discovery blocked?
Use

.

picks another Steam install,

sets the provisioning deadline (default 30s).

,

Was it faster than just picking up the Adapter from where I left it? No. Not even close.
But I now know more about the Steam Frame, the Remote Play protocol and

than I ever wanted to. And you can now (hopefully) use your own 6GHz or 7GHz  (⁶🤷⁷) WiFi card as your "Adapter".

That source-grounded method and the correction are reusable, though the project is educational rather than a new technique.

explanation.grounded: The page supports both claims: animations are mapped to OpenZFS lines pinned at commit 71a9f9578616, and it says the ring holds 128 KiB rather than 128 uberblocks, with slot count set by sector size. These concrete details back the push decision, and the caveat that the project is educational does not undercut it.

A live map you can rewind, that tells you where every contact came from.
There is no shortage of dashboards that draw aircraft and ships on a globe.
Nearly all of them are stateless viewers of somebody else's API: they show you
this instant, they cannot show you last Tuesday, and they render whatever the
upstream asserts without saying who saw it or how long ago. Velocity is
self-hosted and keyless like those, and then does the two things they don't.
It keeps history you own.
Flightradar24 gates replay at 7 days free,

Velocity
A live map you can rewind, that tells you where every contact came from.
There is no shortage of dashboards that draw aircraft and ships on a globe.
Nearly all of them are stateless viewers of somebody else's API: they show you
this instant, they cannot show you last Tuesday, and they render whatever the
upstream asserts without saying who saw it or how long ago. Velocity is
self-hosted and keyless like those, and then does the two things they don't.
It keeps history you own.
Flightradar24 gates replay at 7 days free,
MarineTraffic cut its free window to 24 hours, ADS-B Exchange killed its free
API tier outright, and a self-hosted tool just doesn't have that problem. The
archive is a Postgres + TimescaleDB hypertable (
positions
, 6 hour chunks,
columnar compression segmented by id, plus an hourly
positions_hourly
rollup); migrating the old SQLite file copied 55,352,047 rows at ~120k rows/s
and the compressed hypertable measured 13.46x smaller, 11,300,810,752 bytes
down to 839,786,496. Velocity records position history to your own disk for as
long as you give it room, with a scrubber to rewind to any past moment, and
SQLite remains the keyless fallback when no
HISTORY_PG_DSN
is set. No
account, no API key, nobody who can paywall, filter or cut off your archive.
It scores what it shows you.
Anyone can upload whatever they like to a
crowd-sourced ADS-B aggregator; a contact appearing on a map is not evidence it
was ever broadcast. So every contact carries which independent sources reported
it, how many agreed, and how old the fix actually is — with the confidence rule
written out rather than implied. Cached sources report the age of the
data
,
not the age of the response, so nothing sits on the map looking live because it
was fresh when we fetched it this morning.
/api/status/provenance
gives you
the same picture per source, including how many contacts each one is alone in
seeing.
On top of that: live aircraft, ships, satellites, GPS jamming, dark vessels,
TFR airspace, military bases, naval warnings, earthquakes, outages and conflict
events, correlated on the server instead of leaving you to eyeball six tabs.
Honest scope, since this is a tool for people who check things: coverage is
whatever the public feeds give you, it is not uniform, and the console tells
you where it is thin rather than drawing a confident empty ocean.
And once you've found something worth keeping, it stays evidence: a
chain-of-custody
evidence locker
hashes every capture (a URL snapshot, an
upload, a feed freeze) with SHA-256 and an append-only custody log, then rolls a
case up into a self-contained
HTML / PPTX report
where every claim carries
its provenance. All of it keyless, all of it on your disk.
It also runs as an MCP server, so an AI agent can query the same live feeds
instead of guessing from its training cut-off — everything it returns is
labelled as automated output, not sold as "AI insight."
Quick start

The apps

Take the tour
·

History you can replay

derived

Scope and limits
): the position-history archive, the
local ontology store (objects, case files, situations) and the evidence

Europe (global coverage is sparser and terrestrial-biased), and the 3D

The easy way, with Docker.

compose

Take the tour
1. The whole planet, live.
Thousands of aircraft plus vessels, satellites,
quakes and more on one Cesium globe. Every aircraft and ship renders as its
category icon, coloured and rotated to its heading; dense areas cluster into
count badges you can drill into.
2. Zoom anywhere, toggle everything.
Drag into a region and traffic, labels
and coastlines fill in. The left rail is the whole intel stack in one tree — air,
maritime, space, ground hazards, signals and 18 infrastructure layers — each
with its live count. A right-side map toolbar adds the analyst verbs on top of
the globe:
measure
a running great-circle distance,
area-select
a box
and search every object inside it,
annotate
with dropped markers, or
move
a marker — plus one-click camera reset and zoom.
3. Click anything.
Select an aircraft or vessel and the right panel fills
with its dossier: identity, kinematics, the flight/route, ACARS, a
pattern-of-life baseline, GPS integrity and the raw fields — while a magenta
line traces its recent track on the globe. An
AI assessment
block (labelled,
and grounded in the observed track) summarises what the dossier fields imply.
Click empty space and it all clears.
4. Or query the whole store at once.
The Explorer app is every live object
in one filterable, sortable table — tens of thousands of tracks across vessels,
aircraft and quakes, each tagged with the feed it came from and how long ago it
was seen. Facet it, save the search, export the result to CSV.
5. Chokepoints and AOIs, watched continuously.
A curated library of the
world's maritime chokepoints — Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb, Malacca, the Taiwan
Strait, the English Channel, undersea-cable corridors — each with live transit
counts and the daily oil-flow figures that make it matter. Standing detections
fire against them in the background.
6. Airspace, bases, ports and airports — operational context, still keyless.
Toggle the TFR/Airspace layer and live FAA temporary flight restrictions draw as
real polygons, coloured by reason with their altitude bands. Alongside them:
7,183 military bases (air, naval and army, from Wikidata), NGA NAVAREA broadcast
warnings with mine areas flagged, 3,804 ports from the NGA World Port Index
(harbour size and type, shelter, repairs, dry dock, pier and channel depths),
and airports enriched with runways (length, surface, lighting, per-end ILS
category from FAA NASR), tower/ground/ATIS frequencies, live METAR with flight
category, and a LiveATC linkout. A basemap picker swaps between nine keyless
map styles (Carto dark, 3D satellite + terrain, Apple satellite, Esri
imagery/topo/dark, OpenTopoMap, USGS, Sentinel-2 cloudless), each probed live
before it's offered and each carrying its required attribution.
7. Space, with real physics.
~16k satellites from CelesTrak, propagated
in-browser with actual SGP4 orbital mechanics and enriched from SATCAT with
owner, launch date, radar cross-section and orbit class.
8. The watch officer works the inbox.
An autonomous watch officer fuses
jamming, dark vessels, military air activity and conflict events into ranked,
cited alerts — GPS spoofing, jamming cells, dark-vessel candidates — each with an
[inferred]
reasoning line and a one-click
slew to
. It runs
detect_deception
and
deep_analyze
against the live picture, so the inbox fills itself on a fresh
keyless boot with no operator setup.
9. …and writes the brief.
Every couple of minutes it promotes the
convergences — "vessels went dark near reported activity", "spoofed tracks
co-located with an AIS gap" — into ranked incident cards with a written, cited
summary and a
slew to
button. Actionable incidents are auto-promoted into the
investigation graph, so the ontology grows itself.
10. Keep it as evidence.
Anything worth keeping goes into the
chain-of-custody
evidence locker
: capture a URL snapshot, upload a file, grab
a screenshot, or freeze the current feed state, and each artifact is hashed with
SHA-256, written to
./data/evidence
, and logged to an append-only custody
chain in the local ontology store. Attach it to a situation, re-verify the hash
any time, or roll a whole case into a signed hash-of-hashes manifest. Fully
keyless. From there,
Reports
exports the case (see
Export
) as a
JSON bundle, a self-contained HTML report with per-claim provenance footnotes,
or a PPTX brief — with any AI narrative confined to a clearly labelled block.
11. A tool that draws on the map gets its own window.
The annotation
editor, the watchbox rules and the field kit open as free-floating, draggable,
resizable windows over the globe rather than stealing the rail from the layer
tree — arm a tool from the map toolbar, set up what it draws beside the thing
you are drawing on, and
Window → Re-dock every floating panel
clears them all.
Positions persist for the session.
12. Bring your own data — the Foundry tab.
Upload a CSV/JSON/NDJSON, shape it
through a governed pipeline (13 transform steps: filter, derive, join, aggregate,
union, window, pivot, dedup, cast, sort…), gate every version with data-health
checks (freshness SLAs, schema-drift, uniqueness…), and bind it into the same
ontology graph as the live feeds. Lineage, immutable versions with rollback, and
a dead-letter for rows that fail a transform all come along; the pipeline graph
flags exactly which outputs went stale.
13. Automate it — the Workflows tab.
A node-graph editor over the same live
feeds and ontology: wire sources (aircraft, vessels, quakes, alerts, datasets,
ontology, countries) through sandboxed Python/SQL/LLM transform blocks into sinks
(alerts, ontology objects, datasets, persistent memory), then run it on a
schedule. Control blocks can reach outward too — webhooks to your own server, or
a MAVLink bridge for drone tasking that rehearses log-only without a vehicle.
Scope and limits
The point is fusion. Plenty of sites already do one feed well: Flightradar24 for
planes, MarineTraffic for ships,
GPSJam
for jamming.
Velocity goes after the seam between them: AIS plus radar imagery flags a ship
that's switched its transponder off; a cluster of aircraft reporting bad GPS
integrity becomes a jamming hotspot; when two or more of those line up in the
same place and time, they get promoted to a single incident with a written,
cited summary.
A few things worth knowing up front, because I'd rather you read them here than
be annoyed later:
It's built for one analyst. One optional API key, no accounts or roles.
What persists vs what clears.
Durable under
./data/
or the Timescale
service: the position-history archive (a Postgres + TimescaleDB hypertable by
default; SQLite at
./data/history.db
remains the keyless fallback when no
HISTORY_PG_DSN
is set, with one boot warning naming the switch), the local
ontology store (ontology objects, case files, situations;
intel/ontology_local.py
,
./data/ontology.db
), plus separate SQLite files
for Foundry, Workflows,
alert rules, cached news and the Instability Index scorer (
foundry.db
,
workflows.db
,
alert_rules.db
,
news_history.db
,
instability.db
), and a
keyless-local audit log (
audit_log.db
— only materializes when no
SUPABASE_URL
is configured; a keyed deployment writes audit rows to
Supabase instead and never creates the file). That's 8 SQLite files, not
one — back up the whole
./data
volume, not a single DB. Also durable: the
evidence locker (blobs under
./data/evidence
, custody chain in the
ontology store's append-only
assertions
table), a disk tile cache
(
./data/tilecache
) and any downloaded local models (
./data/models
).
Volatile, and cleared on backend restart: the live incident list, transient
AOI selections, and generated watch-officer briefs. The Docker Compose
volumes mean the durable stores survive
docker compose down
, not just a
process restart.
Retention, honestly.
The dev compose sets
HISTORY_RETENTION_HOURS=48
(2 days), but that's a ceiling, not a promise:
HISTORY_MAX_BYTES
(2 GB by
default) binds first, and at measured global ADS-B+AIS ingest (~3 GB/h on a
keyless box pulling full-breadth feeds) the byte cap fills well before the
hour window matters, leaving well under 2 hours of effective depth out of
the box — not 48. The hour window only becomes the binding limit once disk
is large enough for it to be the tighter cap; a genuine 48h global archive
needs on the order of 150 GB (
~3 GB/h * 48h
). Raise
HISTORY_MAX_BYTES
,
or set
ARCHIVE_MODE=1
with
HISTORY_DISK_BUDGET_GB
sized to what you're
willing to spend on disk (the production compose profile does this, 5 GB to
start).
/api/history/coverage
reports the ACTUAL current depth
(
oldest_ts
), not the configured ceiling, and the 2D console's day-picker
and ownership chip render it, so you can see what you're really getting.
Depth answers now come from the hourly
positions_hourly
aggregate; the old
SQLite coverage scan took 73 s over 78M fixes, which is why the rollup
exists.
AIS runs keyless and global (~50k vessels tracked, MMSI-deduped across
ShipXplorer, MyShipTracking, Digitraffic and Kystverket), but coverage is densest over
Northern Europe and the Baltic and thins out elsewhere; an AISStream key fills
in the gaps. Sparse regions still lean on the radar (SAR) layer.
The two headless-Chrome sidecars are degraded under Docker, not crashed.
ADS-B (OpenSky + the httpx tar1090 mirrors + ShipXplorer AIS) and the
regional Kystverket/Digitraffic AIS feeds are direct HTTP calls and run at
full strength in the container. But the tar1090 ADS-B sidecar and
MyShipTracking (the enabled primary keyless
wide-area
AIS source) drive a
real Chromium via Node, which the slim API image doesn't ship — they log a
warning and sit idle rather than crash the backend, so you lose their extra
coverage, not the app. Run bare-metal (
bash scripts/run-api.sh
) for full
sidecar coverage.

What is enforced
Not promises, checks in the tree. Each line names the route or test that holds
it:
Clearance on reads and writes.
One predicate,
intel/ontology.visible_to
, filters local reads (
get
,
list_by_kind
,
search
, links, assertions) and the situations, maps and evidence routes by
the caller's level and compartments; keyless callers are clearance 0, and a
write above clearance or onto a hidden row answers 403.
→
apps/api/tests/test_clearance_local_reads.py
Custody-chained evidence.
Every capture is hashed with SHA-256 and
appended to an immutable custody log;
GET /api/evidence/{sha}/verify
re-checks the bytes. →
apps/api/tests/test_evidence.py
Hash-chained audit.
Mutations append to
action_log.db
;
GET /api/audit/verify
walks the chain. →
apps/api/tests/test_asvs_fix_a_logging.py
Citations withheld when ungrounded.
LLM_REQUIRE_CITATIONS=1
(default)
withholds a selection or country brief that cites none of its own ids;
GET /api/ai/guardrails
reports the posture. →
apps/api/tests/test_citations_hard.py
Human-in-the-loop write-back.
A write-back action is operator-only and
runs only from a proposal the operator approves; the audit row carries the
payload's SHA-256, never the payload. →
apps/api/tests/test_writeback_action.py

MCP server: query the live console from an AI agent
The part I think is genuinely new: the backend doubles as a
Model Context
Protocol
server, so an AI agent can interrogate the same warm feeds the globe
renders without scraping a dozen sites or flooding its own context. Ask "where
is GPS being jammed right now?" and it answers from the live feed. Full
architecture +
/api/intel/*
HTTP reference:
docs/mcp-server.md
.
It exposes 94 tools over
app.mcp_server
(a representative slice below; run
--list-tools
for the full set):
Tool
What it returns
get_situation
Global summary: aircraft by category, GNSS-degraded count, emergencies, worst jamming cells, vessel/alert counts. The cheap first call.
focus_area(lat,lon,radius_nm)
Loads a region PRIMARY
(dedicated fresh
/v2/point
fetch + ongoing priority refresh, independent of global rate limits) and returns a full bundle: aircraft + density + GPS jamming + vessels + fused anomalies.
aircraft_density
Grid of cells (count, by category, GNSS-degraded) for an area.
gps_jamming
GPSJam-method assessment (ADS-B NACp<8 / NIC<7, 1° bins): flagged cells, severity, affected aircraft. Global or scoped.
query_aircraft
Filtered query (bbox/centre, category, squawk, callsign, altitude band, emergency / gnss_degraded / on_ground).
lookup_aircraft(ident)
One aircraft by ICAO24 or callsign + integrity/threat assessment.
query_vessels
AIS vessels in an area, classified;
dark_only
for dark-vessel candidates.
anomalies
Fused report: emergencies, jamming hotspots, dark vessels, alerts + a triage threat level.
detect_deception
/
locate_emitter
Flag spoofed/co-located tracks; triangulate a jamming source from degraded-integrity aircraft.
whats_changed
/
incident_history
Delta since a timestamp; the incident timeline for an area.
deep_analyze(question, lat?, lon?)
Gathers the relevant intel JSON and has a
reasoning model
reason over it (DeepSeek when configured, else a local Ollama model), so heavy analysis stays off the agent's context and only the conclusion returns.
Every tool returns compact, bounded JSON (counts, grids, ≤50-item samples), so
an agent can sweep the planet for a few hundred tokens instead of pulling 15k
features. Heavy tools also take
detail='short'
(the default digest — top-N
of each list plus a
<field>_total
) or
detail='long'
(the full bundle), so
an agent sweeps in
short
and drills in
long
. Area-primary loading means the
agent's region of interest stays fresh and dense even while the global firehose is
being rate-limited; the rest of the world keeps streaming from the sticky snapshot.

System requirements
The heavy component is the
client
, a CesiumJS WebGL2 globe. It is GPU- and
browser-main-thread-bound, and the backend is light. WebGL2 is required
(Chrome/Edge 110+, Firefox 110+). On hybrid-graphics laptops, force the discrete
GPU (
chrome://gpu
, look for adapter "ACTIVE").

Now live:
the Pipe IDE runs right in your browser — build, run, and visually debug your programs, no install needed.
Try Pipe IDE — No Account Required
Frequently Asked Questions
Do we need to rewrite our existing system in Pipe?
To some extent, yes — but the transition is far less disruptive than it sounds:
The migration is gradual — you don't have to discard all existing code at once.
You start by wrapping your entire project in a single top-level block. That's the initial step. Then, whenever you're ready, you add a workflow inside that top-level block and distribute the code across the visual blocks of the newly created workflow — and you can keep going, level by level.
You choose how far to go.
You can stop subdividing blocks at any point, so it's entirely your decision which parts of the system become visual and which remain as text.
Pipe makes integration easy.
It provides a simple bridge for connecting visual blocks to your existing text code.
AI reduces the overhead of going visual.
AI can generate diagram layouts from your existing code, update them as the code changes, suggest how to partition logic across blocks, and flag structural issues as your model grows.
We tried visual programming before, and it didn't work.
Every technology advances in a spiral — it fails several times before its lessons are learned and it finally succeeds. Pipe was built by studying exactly why earlier visual languages fell short. Two lessons in particular shaped it:
A visual language must be both general-purpose and semantically powerful to compete with text.
Text-based languages dominate precisely because they have both qualities; any visual language that lacks either will fail. Pipe has both.
The answer isn't to swing between extremes.
We tried pure visual programming, it didn't work, so we went back to text-only — which has its own problems, now made obvious by AI. Good engineering doesn't jump between extremes; it finds a synthesis that keeps the strengths of each while minimizing their weaknesses. That's Pipe's core philosophy: it doesn't replace text-based languages — it complements them. In practice, that means the developer decides what goes into visual diagrams and what stays as text.
Why now?

Table of Contents
A devbox task or app that asks for `gpu="AppleSilicon"` now runs natively on your Mac, so `torch.device("mps")` and MLX work the way `"cuda"` does on a cluster.
The Flyte devbox is where I iterate on ML code before it goes anywhere near a cluster: `flyte start devbox`, write a task, run it, look at it in the console. On an Apple Silicon Mac there's been one glaring gap. The devbox runs every task and app in a container, and on a Mac that container is a Linux VM. Linux has no Metal, so `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` is `False` in there, MLX doesn't run at all, and the 40-core GPU on my laptop sits idle while my training loop crawls along on the CPU.
So we added an Apple Silicon accelerator to the devbox. You ask for it the way you'd ask for an A100:
Copied to clipboard!
env = flyte.TaskEnvironment(
name="apple-silicon-train",
image=flyte.Image.from_debian_base().with_pip_packages("torch", "torchvision"),
resources=flyte.Resources(cpu=2, memory="4Gi", gpu="AppleSilicon"),
)
and start the devbox with one flag:
Copied to clipboard!
flyte start devbox --apple-silicon
That's the whole API. `gpu=flyte.APPLE_SILICON()` is the same request if you prefer the device helpers (`flyte.GPU`, `flyte.TPU`, `flyte.AMD_GPU`).
What actually runs where
The obvious design is to pass the GPU through to the container. That isn't possible: there's no Metal inside a Linux VM to pass anything to. An earlier version of this work kept the task in its container and gave it a host-side MLX model server to call over HTTP. That's useful if all you want is completions, but it means your code can't touch the GPU itself. You can't move a PyTorch model to `mps`, you can't train, and you can't load an arbitrary Hugging Face model.
So the default is the other way around.
The workload's code runs natively on the Mac
, and the container becomes its proxy:
The container starts as usual. Its Flyte entrypoint (`a0` for tasks, `fserve` for apps) sees that the backend scheduled it as an Apple Silicon workload and hands its own invocation to a bridge that `flyte start devbox --apple-silicon` runs on the host.
The bridge builds a cached `uv` environment for macOS from the image's pip packages, rewrites the in-cluster endpoints to the devbox ports the Mac can reach, and runs the same entrypoint there.
The container streams the host process's log, mirrors its exit code, forwards aborts, and for apps forwards its port, so the console, the run's logs and the app URL behave as they would for any other workload.
From the console's perspective, a task ran in a pod and produced outputs. From the Mac's perspective, a Python process ran in `~/.flyte/apple-silicon/envs/...` with the GPU right there.
On the backend side, a pod that requests the `APPLE_SILICON` device class gets no GPU resource request (no device plugin could satisfy it, so it would sit `Pending` forever) and no GPU node affinity. Instead it gets the bridge's endpoint and a per-workload HMAC token, so one workload can't talk to another's process.

Once the code is on the Mac, the training loop is ordinary PyTorch. The only Apple-specific line is the device:
Copied to clipboard!
@env.task
async def train(epochs: int = 3, batch_size: int = 256, lr: float = 1e-3) -> tuple[dict, flyte.io.File]:
import torch
...
# On a cluster this would be "cuda"; on the Mac's GPU it is "mps". Fail rather than train on the CPU.
if not torch.backends.mps.is_available():
raise RuntimeError("mps is not available: run with gpu='AppleSilicon' on an Apple Silicon devbox")
device = torch.device("mps")
...
model = nn.Sequential(...).to(device)

The task's own `print` lines show up in the run's logs in the console, streamed from the process on the Mac.
The first run takes a few minutes because the bridge has to build the macOS environment (torch, torchvision) and download MNIST. Later runs reuse both.

requires_auth=False,

No more forking Tree-sitter grammars.
Powderworks provides professionally maintained, well-tested Tree-sitter compatible Wasm grammars for security and code analysis, with comprehensive coverage of all the languages you care about.
The Tree-sitter ecosystem is great for editors. Its grammars are fast, incremental, and forgiving: they keep highlighting while you type and patch over code they don't understand. Static analysis needs something else. A SAST tool has to read every file the way the language's own tooling does, in the language version the project actually uses, and a grammar that patches or skips over code it doesn't understand means missed findings and false alarms.

When a grammar doesn't know a new syntax or a dialect your customers write, you patch your own copy and wait, hoping that the next upstream release will happen sometime this year and address your issue. A single grammar for every version gets some of these wrong whichever version your project uses, and the scanner, linter, or migration tool built on it misreads your code.
